questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I chose to go on exchange because I have always wanted to use that opportunity while I could, and COVID-19 ruined my exchange plans on my bachelor. Also, I was recommended to go on exchange as it was considered a big plus for both academic and career opportunities.
I choose Leiden in The Netherlands because I have never been to The Netherlands in the first place. The next question before I choose Leiden was: where to go in The Netherlands?
I picked Amsterdam as my 1. priority, Leiden as my 2. priority and Rotterdam as my 3. priority. I ended up receiving a spot at Leiden University. I choose Leiden due to my gut feeling. I have never been to The Netherlands, so I had no experience or information on to base any informed choice. During my initial research on Leiden, I just had a good feeling. I liked the courses I could pick, I liked the city as it was beautiful and the geographic location made it a perfect spot to explore the Netherlands, located just between The Hague and Amsterdam with less than 30 minutes both ways. Also, all the reports from other students spoke very highly of Leiden and I have heard good things about The Netherlands as a culture and country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can highly recommend Leiden University as your destination as it is an extremely international student-friendly city, but please bear in mind my recommendations and comments in this report as I did experience some rather frustrating difficulties.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was okay easy. The websites were a bit difficult to navigate, but everything was in English. Also, the local coordinators were good to remind you by e-mail if you needed to do something or forgot anything. So I never experienced the shock of missing out on any vital information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
On my way to Leiden, I was on my own. I had to find the address and all that by myself. Luckily I meet a very friendly German girl, who was going the same way as I was. Leiden University boasted that they had a stand to help with info at the airport, but I never found it.
A local student organization organised what they call an OWL-week, which is an introductory week for all international students. That was extremely helpful in making new friends, getting to know the city, getting a bike, and all the necessary preparations for my stay. It was also very good fun.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The Netherlands don't accept VISA or Mastercard most places, so be prepared for that. Cash or get a Maestro card. I used Revolut

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding housing in Leiden is EXTREMELY difficult. I cannot exaggerate how tough it was. I found my housing a week before departure. I almost didn't go. Please be proactive on Facebook or other social media, there are also many dutch websites that connect people. Create a profile on those at your first opportunity. Also, create a profile on the local DUWO website as soon as you can. Don't be picky! Start as soon as you are sure you are going to Leiden.

Also, don't apply for the big local student houses. They are fraternities or sororities and do not accept non-dutch students. I only heard of one which got accepted, and there are hundreds of new international students in Leiden each season.

I also recommend paying for the housing option through the University, when you apply. Be quick about it, as it is first come, first served. You can only apply for housing after you have registered for courses. You can always change courses, so pick some fast. Also, if you don't get anything on the first round, don't accept the refund, wait, as there is most likely a second round if there are more available rooms. That is how I got mine. I was lucky. Some were homeless for the first month of their stay. There is no on-site service at the University.

Best advice, don't be picky. Say yes to the first and best option.

I stayed at a dorm at Hugo de Grootstraat 32, which I can recommend, which I got through DUWO, but at the last minute.

Economics:
Finding on our own can be the cheapest option, but you have the most security on your housing with booking through DUWO or the university.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I also highly recommend finding something in Leiden itself, as it makes your life easier with going to the university daily and also with all the social events. Many ended up though in surrounding areas around Leiden, which is just as fine if you have a bike. The Hague is also a viable option but is tricky due to transport time.
Leiden is easy to navigate if you have a bike. There is no on-campus housing at all.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing was good, but I give it a 2 just due to the extreme difficulty of acquiring one. Very frustrating and stressful process, but it is worth it if you get housing in the end.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
If you study communication and IT as I do, you gonna have some difficulties registering for courses, but it worked out in the end, but at that time I was already a month into my stay.

I still highly recommend Leiden though, as it most worth it after you have passed the registering process

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
They perceive you as a humanities student due to our study being located on KUA, but all the communication and IT courses at Leiden University are on the science campus in which we are familiar or have skills in. Also, the deal between KU and Leiden, is that we request at least 15 EC points for humanities courses during our stay. If you care about your courses for academic purposes, then think twice about Leiden, as there are only two courses on the humanities faculty that make sense for our line of study. The last 15 EC points are free choice.
Since they are in doubt of our academic profile, you will get rejected for all humanities courses when you seek approval. Arrange a meeting with the coordinator the first chance you get to address this problem. Also, just apply for every single humanities course when you apply, as they will most likely pick the course they think is best for you as they course based on available seats. I had no say in what humanities courses I ended up having.
Very frustrating process.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There are two coordinators on site who can help, but they are overburdened and help is slow. If you get into any trouble, then go to them physically or arrange a meeting. It speeds up the process. Patience is key.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not at all. I don't know if it was a lack of supervision or whatever. They ended up choosing my humanities courses for me, as my academic profile did not fit with any of the courses as most courses had some sort of required pre-acquired knowledge or earlier taken course. I choose for myself three courses that made sense for our line of study, at the science faculty, but those were tough, and only do it if you are motivated, as they will take a lot of your time.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Leiden's selection of courses for exchange students on a master level is vague and most don't make sense for my line of study. Ergo, Leiden is best for bachelor students looking to go on exchange.
There is an approval process after you have picked your courses. Ergo, you are not guaranteed anything. So apply for as many as you can or want, to make the process easier in the end.
Also, if you want to have the freest time to explore and delve into the culture. Pick three courses with 10 EC points. I choose 5 courses with fewer points, and I spend almost as much time on those as I would have had on 5 courses with 10 EC points.
Also, the science courses make the most sense for our line of study, but are difficult and require a level of maths that we do not have. I you go that way, be prepared.
The best advice, apply for all courses you find interesting, as you will most likely get rejected by almost all of them.
Also, pay attention to the prerequisites for each course and registering process, as some courses require special registration at the master level. Also, some course descriptions are vague and you might be surprised. Again, don't be picky. Also, stay for courses at the humanities faculty if you are going on exchange for the experience and not the academia.
Also, make sure that the coordinators know you need 30 EC points. Some students from other countries don't, so it is not a given.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Leiden has a high level of academics. I learned so much, but they expects things from you if you are a master student.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Science courses are difficult. Humanities less so. Most, I learned, choose humanities courses to make it easier for them. I thought that I could take it easy with some of the courses. Turns out, the grading in Leiden is way tougher than KU, and therefore slacking was not an option in order to pass.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was very different. The grading system is different. The assignment requirements are a max number of words. Also, your total grade over the course of the semester varies in each course, as each course's grading is up to the teacher. Be aware of that.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Machine Learning
Managing software evolution
Computation creativity
Language, culture and cognition
Language documentation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Pick the ones with the easiest exam or semester plan, as you most likely will have little influence over which courses you end up having. I ended up spending to much time on my studies, and therefore I did not get to do all I wanted.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spend around 25.000 DKK each month. The level of social events and activities blew my mind and my bank account, but it was good fun. Also, they are several trips and events to go on, and they cost money. I also went on several international trips, and they were quite expensive. It is possible to spend a lot less than I did.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transport was expensive.
The food and beer were cheaper.
Otherwise pretty much the same as in DK.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They are so many activities you can take part in. The amount of those was insane. There was something for everybody. Sports, clubs, books, cooking, etc. There was everything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do some sports and join the ESN events and parties. Also, don't be afraid to go alone to things, most others do that as well. You will not be disappointed.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore the country. Go out. Go see the culture. Make trips with your new friends. There is a lot to see and do. Also, make a journal of the all things you do. Will make it much easier to explain what you did to your friends and family.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The dutch do some things differently than we do, but in general, the culture is pretty much the same as here in Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to say hi. Most are also looking for friends. Remember to cross boundaries and be open-minded. Go to the events!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
No challenges. Leiden is lovely, and everybody is very nice!
But, remember to acquire a maestro card! Most places don't accept VISA or Mastercard.
Everybody speaks English.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The dutch people are very social. Expect a lot of social and cultural events. They are also very helpfull.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get a maestro card!
If you are a master's student in communication and IT, don't be picky with your courses and expect difficulties. If you are a bachelor, go for it.
GO FOR HOUSING ASAP! I cannot stress this enough. Some were homeless and staying with friends for the first couple of weeks.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The Netherlands is a crowded place. It is the same size as Denmark, but 3 times the population, which means a lot of big cities, etc. Go out of Leiden and see the country. You will not be disappointed. 
Get a bike!
Get an OV-chipkaart. Will make traveling much easier.
Get the Maestro Card!!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the new friends I got, all the things I saw and did, and the experience of being alone in a new country. It was also 4 months but felt like a year. So much happened!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Entertaining myself. Finding groups for projects on my own. Finding time to do all I wanted.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
